note_claims.claim: The patient presents with a dry cough lasting approximately 2 months.
The patient has a persistent dry, tickly, non-productive cough.
The patient has no history of haemoptysis, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss.
The patient has no history of breathlessness or chest pain.
The patient has no history of heartburn, voice change, or dysphagia.
The patient started ramipril in late May for hypertension.
The ramipril dose was increased from 2.5 mg to 5 mg in July.
The cough began after starting ramipril.
The patient is an ex-smoker who previously smoked about 10 cigarettes a day for approximately 15 years (7.5 pack-years).
The patient is currently taking ramipril 5 mg once daily.
The patient is taking atorvastatin 20 mg at night.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
The chest examination is clear bilaterally.
The patient's blood pressure is 134/82.
The persistent dry cough is most likely induced by an ACE inhibitor.
The plan is to stop ramipril and switch the patient to losartan 50 mg once daily.
A blood test for kidneys and salt levels is required 1–2 weeks after starting losartan.
A chest X-ray is recommended due to the patient being an ex-smoker with a 2-month cough.
The patient is advised that the cough may take up to 3 months to resolve after stopping ramipril.
The patient is advised to contact the practice sooner if they experience haemoptysis, breathlessness, unintentional weight loss, or chest pain.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician greeted the patient, Mr Penhaligon, and asked if he had brought someone with him.
The patient's wife, Margaret, is present.
The relative stated that someone has to do the remembering.
The patient's complaint is a dry, tickly cough that never stops.
The patient has had the cough for about six weeks.
The cough started before the patient's sister's birthday, which was early August.
The patient corrected the relative, stating it was more like two months.
The cough is completely dry, and the patient is not bringing anything up.
The patient denies any blood.
The patient denies fevers, night sweats, or losing weight.
The patient stated they put on a bit of weight.
The patient denies breathlessness or chest pain, and is fine walking the dog.
The patient denies heartburn or acid coming up into the throat.
The patient denies any change in voice or trouble swallowing.
The patient gave up smoking 20 years ago, but previously smoked about ten a day for maybe fifteen years.
The clinician referenced the patient's record showing they started ramipril for blood pressure in the summer, specifically June.
The relative recalled ramipril started at the end of May because they had just returned from Whitby.
The patient corrected the dose information, stating they are now taking five milligrams once a day, and that the dose was increased from 2.5 mg in July.
The patient is taking atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night.
The patient denies any known drug allergies.
The relative mentioned that she coughs at night, but her condition is asthma.
The clinician stated they would ensure only Geoff's chest was noted in his records.
The patient denies ever having asthma.
The clinician examined the patient's chest and throat, finding them clear and normal.
The clinician measured the patient's blood pressure as 134 over 82.
The clinician suggested that ramipril might be causing the cough because it is a well-known side effect, and the timing fits (cough started after starting ramipril).
The clinician suggested stopping ramipril and switching the patient to losartan 50 mg once a day.
The clinician planned to start losartan at 50 milligrams once a day.
The clinician planned to order a blood test to check kidneys and salt levels one to two weeks after starting losartan.
The clinician planned to see the patient again in four weeks to check blood pressure.
The clinician advised that the cough may take up to three months to settle after stopping ramipril.
The clinician suggested arranging a chest X-ray to be thorough, given the patient's history as an ex-smoker and the duration of the cough.
The clinician advised the patient to contact the practice sooner if they cough up any blood, become short of breath, lose weight without trying, or get any chest pain.
The clinician stated that if the cough has not improved at all by the four-week review, they will think again about other causes.
